prime.problem: The same open model runs at 48 tokens/s on one host and 1,745 on another, and at 15 on your laptop. Without a picture of where bandwidth comes from you can't tell a real speed advantage from a marketing number, or decide whether buying hardware is worth it.
prime.fits: Second mechanism card: the bandwidth side of the memory-bandwidth division. Quantization and MoE, next, work on the bytes side.
prime.goal: Place any chip on the bandwidth ladder and predict roughly how fast a model can write on it, and why a host may deliver much less than that.

attend: Why do Groq and Cerebras keep weights in on-chip SRAM, and what does that cost them in capacity?
Why does a 34× bandwidth gap (M3 vs H100) not translate into 34× faster answers on cheap hosts?
Why is an RTX 4090's 10× bandwidth less useful than it sounds for big models?
For an 80-token answer, why does host hardware barely matter?

must: Hardware sets memory bandwidth → bandwidth sets the tokens/s ceiling → laptop 100 GB/s, H100 3.35 TB/s, SRAM chips 80+ TB/s to 21 PB/s → the ceiling spans orders of magnitude
SRAM sits on the chip next to the compute → far more bandwidth but little capacity (44 GB per Cerebras wafer) → big models must be split across many chips → only a short list of models is served
A host shares each chip across many users to cut cost → your slice of the bandwidth shrinks → cheap H100 hosts deliver 48–90 t/s despite a ~1,240 t/s single-user ceiling
elevated: Capacity decides what fits, bandwidth decides how fast → a 24 GB RTX 4090 has 10× the M3's bandwidth but can't hold big models without heavy quantization
reference: the exact bandwidth of each chip (M4 Max 546 GB/s, H200 4.8 TB/s, B200 ~8 TB/s)

compress.prompt: From memory, sketch the bandwidth ladder with at least five rungs and their rough bandwidths, and mark where the 653-token FizzBuzz answer takes 42 s, 13.6 s and 0.37 s. Then write two sentences on why the same weights can be 36× apart.
checklist: M3 100 GB/s → H100 3.35 TB/s → SRAM chips 80+ TB/s / 21 PB/s
sharing (batch size), quantization and speculative decoding also differ by host
for short answers, TTFT and network dominate instead

retrieve.q: Explain why on-chip SRAM makes Groq and Cerebras so fast, and what limits it.
answer: SRAM on the chip delivers far more bandwidth than off-chip memory
so reading the weights per token is much faster
but capacity is small, so large models are spread across many chips and only a few models are offered

retrieve.q: Walk through why gpt-oss-120b on a cheap GPU host runs at 48 t/s when the single-user H100 ceiling is about 1,240 t/s.
answer: the host batches many users per GPU, so each gets a fraction of the bandwidth
plus overhead, attention and KV-cache reads: 48–334 t/s measured on GPU hosts

retrieve.q: Your answers average 80 tokens. Is paying extra for a latency-tuned host worth it over a 48 t/s standard host? What about for 2,000-token answers?
answer: 80 tokens at 48 t/s ≈ 1.7 s; TTFT and network dominate, so little to gain
2,000 tokens: 41.7 s at 48 t/s vs about 1.1 s at 1,745 t/s: a big win
also weigh price, quantization and which models the fast host serves

compare.q: Faster hardware and quantization both raise the tokens/s ceiling. Which side of the division does each change, and what does each one cost you?
answer: hardware raises bandwidth (numerator); quantization cuts bytes per token (denominator)
hardware costs money (or a host change and network); quantization costs accuracy
they stack: a quantized model on a faster chip gets both

compare.q: This card treats a chip as one bandwidth number. What does the GPU-as-a-machine view add (memory hierarchy, compute units), and when does the one-number model mislead?
answer: the GPU has a hierarchy: HBM, on-chip caches/shared memory, registers
one number is right for batch-1 decode that streams weights from HBM
it misleads when data is reused on-chip (prefill, big batches) and compute becomes the limit

predict.q: A new laptop chip doubles the M3's bandwidth to 200 GB/s. Predict qwen3.5:4b's speed on it from the M3's measured 15.4 t/s, and say whether you'd expect exactly 2×.
predict.answer: About 30 t/s if the same 44% of the ceiling is reached (200 ÷ 2.85 ≈ 70 t/s ceiling × 0.44). Probably a bit less than 2×: the Apple chip table showed the share of ceiling falling as bandwidth rose (75% → 58%), since fixed software overheads take a bigger slice as each token gets faster.

apply.task: Pick a model you'd like to run and three places it could run: your own machine, a standard cloud host and a latency-tuned host. For each, compute the bandwidth ceiling (bandwidth ÷ bytes per token), look up or estimate the delivered speed, and compute the writing time for a 653-token answer. Decide which one you'd choose for a chat app and for a nightly batch job.
apply.done: You have a three-row table with ceiling, delivered speed and 653-token time, and a one-line choice for each workload that mentions more than speed (price, privacy or model availability).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether doubling bandwidth doubles speed?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why SRAM hosts serve only a few models?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: bandwidth → ceiling, or sharing → delivered speed?
Would buying hardware actually be your best speed lever? Why or why not?
What do you expect quantization to do to the other side of the division?
